examples.category_label: Provisional release omits required Finance approval
examples.category_authorship: Assistant-proposed exact label explicitly accepted by the user.
evidence_scope_notes: The quoted provisional-release clause names Program Manager and Purchase only; approved record17 requires Finance controllers, Program managers and Purchase, all three.
Counterevidence: the immediately following paragraph explicitly requires all three approvers and instructs platform routing to enforce that rule; every tier also includes Finance.
The reviewer identifies a potential authorization/routing and commitment risk. No platform implementation, actual approval bypass or expenditure was observed.
The claim that the exception becomes the normal route is the reviewer’s prospective hypothesis, not a measured frequency.

The draft says release is subject to a cap and leaves its value for CPO decision. It does not specify whether an unset cap blocks release, so unlimited authorization or actual uncapped exposure is not established.
TechSol’s eventual implementation and the CPO’s understanding are projected consequences, not observed behavior.
The reviewer explicitly confirmed the category and minimum correction. No repair experiment or platform implementation has occurred; a separate severity scale was not elicited.
examples.output_evidence: Section5, flexibility point(4), packet page6: “Provisional release: for urgent program needs, the vendor can proceed at a provisional price, subject to a cap, while the final price is settled. This must be recorded and approved by the Program Manager and Purchase.”
examples.source_and_consequence:
Approval authority: Finance controllers can be bypassed on any urgent change. That is the typical late-change case the redesign targets, so the exception would become the normal route. TechSol would build the two-role routing into the platform, and the CPO would approve the workflow believing the three-way rule covers every price.
Cost: production, tooling and materials can commit at a provisional price before Finance sees it. The later “final price” approval then comes after the money is spent and risks becoming a formality. The cap is undefined, an open point left to the CPO, so exposure is uncapped until it is set.
examples.minimum_repair: Require Finance, Program Manager and Purchase approval before any provisional release. Configure the platform to block release until the cap is defined and all three approvals are recorded.
examples.minimum_repair_authorship: Assistant-proposed wording explicitly accepted by the user.

examples.category_label: Tooling release not gated on bridge supply
examples.category_authorship: Exact label explicitly supplied and confirmed by the user for Case4.
evidence_scope_notes: This is the reviewer’s conditional production-interruption scenario, not an observed line stoppage.
The source states tooling ownership but not one tooling set, absence of duplicates, or available molded stock.
Day14-45 combines inspection, transfer and trials. Departure around day14-20 is the reviewer’s interpretation, not an explicit source release date.
ScenarioB proposes a six-month supply tail; the operative source states no extension has been agreed.

The reviewer explicitly confirmed the category and minimum correction for this case. The earlier issue-only buffer-stock judgment remains separate and was not silently reaffirmed as the primary full-output finding.
The reviewer clarified that the estimate uses the evaluated output’s own4.5-5month gap counted from day21. This time basis is not independent ground truth.

The user confirmed the arithmetic as a conditional illustration, optimistic on build-ahead, with full21-day production and unit/set equivalence explicitly assumed. These assumptions are not source-confirmed facts.
Zero opening stock is assumed; available opening stock would reduce the shortage. The case’s actual stock remains unknown.
The2410-2810set range is a conditional illustration using the output’s4.5-5month gap; it is not a measured loss or a forecast of the exact early-transfer schedule.
examples.output_evidence: Section 4 timeline, Day 14-45 (Engineering / Quality): “Tooling inspection and transfer (about 25 days), then trials at the new plastics supplier.”
examples.source_and_consequence:
ase 4’s “Day 14-45” tooling-transfer row ships the plastic tool out of LPI around day 14–20, before the 21-day notice ends, so LPI can’t supply a bridge even though Scenario B promises a 6-month supply tail. With local supply not ready until month 5–6, roughly 2,400–2,800 sets (about 3–3.5 months of Modlev demand) would have no source, assuming no opening stock and LPI’s best-case build-ahead, which would halt the line.

Reviewer clarification of the estimate’s time basis:
**Not exactly.** It uses Case 4’s own stated gap, “about 4.5 to 5 months between the end of the notice period and local supply” (Section 1), counted from day 21.

Reviewer confirmation and qualification of the conditional illustration:
**Yes, with the conditions spelled out.** “Optimistic” is right for LPI’s output, but opening stock cuts the other way. I’d label it “conditional illustration, optimistic on build-ahead.”
examples.minimum_repair: Separate the bridge and no-bridge plans. For the bridge plan, gate tooling release on LPI’s final molding run and verified supply coverage, then update transfer and qualification dates. For the no-bridge plan, explicitly identify any uncovered production gap.

examples.category_definition: plastic tool scheduled to move on days 21-46 while the 5-6 month LPI bridge still needs it
examples.category_authorship: Explicit user-provided category; assistant normalization changes spaces to underscores for storage only.
evidence_scope_notes: The single-tooling-set condition is the reviewer’s stated assumption. The source does not explicitly establish one set, rule out duplicates, or quantify existing molded stock.
The user supplied exact passages and practical consequences; no additional why question is needed.
Earlier content_acceptable=yes was explicitly superseded by content_acceptable=no; raw answer history is preserved.
Formal category supplied by the reviewer; minimum repair explicitly confirmed by the reviewer. No repair intervention has been run. Native-file/page-length compliance remains unverified.
examples.output_evidence:
Section 5 timeline, Day 21-46 (Purchase / Logistics), packet page 5: “Tooling transfer to India (about 25 days) if LPI agrees to release it or it is exercised.”
Section 3 tooling ask, packet page 4: “Release of tooling on request, with the 25-day transfer window”.
Section 1 bridge objective, packet page 3: “a bridge supply of about 5-6 months from LPI”.
Section 4 backup supply, packet page 4: “Cover the gap with stock built before LPI stops, any partial shipments, and spot and air purchases.”
examples.source_and_consequence:
- Section 1 sets the objective as “a bridge supply of about 5-6 months from LPI,” and the “Month 5-6” row has LiIon phasing out LPI then.
- With one plastic tool set, the tool can’t both be moving to India on days 21-46 and be molding lamps at LPI for months afterward. The timeline assumes both.
- Nothing gates the tool move on LPI’s final plastics run or a last-time buy. Case 2 has that gate (“Move tooling only after replacement coverage and the final LPI molding batch are secured”).
- The sentence is conditional, but reading it as “only if LPI agrees” doesn’t fix the plan. The fixed day 21-46 slot and the “Months 1-4” plastics re-development row both assume the tool arrives by about day 46. If release waits until the bridge ends, those rows slip.
- In the no-bridge case the move is the right BATNA action. But then the secondary passage in Section 4 has no identified source: “Cover the gap with stock built before LPI stops, any partial shipments, and spot and air purchases.”
examples.minimum_repair: Separate the bridge and no-bridge plans. For the bridge plan, gate tooling release on LPI’s final molding run and verified supply coverage, then update transfer and qualification dates. For the no-bridge plan, explicitly identify any uncovered production gap.
